review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Depression disorder is a global health crisis, due to its high prevalence. Yet clinical treatments are inadequate. Uncovering the neural correlates of depression remission is a vital step toward developing effective therapies. Using a method termed therapeutic network mapping, we performed secondary analyses on the data of 16 longitudinal experiments and found that the network of the amygdala was commonly modulated by three antidepressant therapies (pharmacotherapy, electroconvulsive therapy, and magnetic seizure therapy). This therapeutic network was i) validated by two independent treatment datasets of patients with depression and a prospective preclinical experiment on male rats, ii) associated with networks of depression-related genes, neurotransmitters, and cognitions, and iii) also the target network of deep brain stimulation and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS). Finally, a longitudinal rTMS experiment indicated that strengthened therapeutic network connectivity is associated with higher depressant alleviation. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that distinct antidepressant therapies act on a common network with potential targets for developing effective therapies.

---

## Introduction

Depression disorder represents a severe global health crisis, owing to its high prevalence1,2. It is a leading contributor to disability and premature mortality in the world3,4. Pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy are first-line treatments for depression disorder. However, the therapeutic effects typically require weeks to months of continuous treatment to manifest, and approximately 30% of patients do not respond to these treatments5. These refractory patients need more intensive interventions6, such as electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), and magnetic seizure therapy (MST). Although these clinical therapies are effective, their mechanisms remain largely unknown.

Longitudinal imaging studies can provide important clues to understanding the remission mechanism of depression7. Relative to the highly variable workflows for functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)8, methods in structural studies are more homogeneous. However, the findings of such studies are inconsistent. For instance, MST was found to increase gray matter volume (GMV) in the bilateral paracentral lobule9, but ECT studies found restricted volume changes in the hippocampus–amygdala complex10,11 or widespread alterations in the brain12. The diversity of these findings between and within therapies has been a major obstacle to understanding the mechanism of depression remission. Regarding these findings as functionally isolated regions, coordinate-based meta-analytic approaches such as activation likelihood estimation are powerful tools for identifying the most consistent results13,14. Nonetheless, it is increasingly evident that brain regions linked to symptom remission are not acting in isolation. Rather, they are linked through distributed functional and structural brain circuits7,15–17. For instance, the targets of deep brain stimulation (DBS) and rTMS for depression belong to the same functional brain network18. Here, we hypothesized that the heterogeneous brain changes across different depression therapies aggregate in a common brain network.

Lesion network mapping is an effective way to determine the network effect of local changes19. This technique uses brain lesions as seeds to delineate the resting-state functional network of specific symptoms based on a normative connectome. This powerful and broadly applicable technique20 has been extended by replacing brain lesions with coordinates of brain structural atrophy21–23 and brain stimulation sites18,24 as seeds. Adapted from this technique, we propose a new method—called therapeutic network mapping—to identify the common network modulated by different therapies for depression. Briefly, we transformed the brain regions that longitudinally changed after treatment to networks through normative resting-state functional connectomes25,26 and explored the common connectivity across distinct therapies.

This study aimed to test whether distinct antidepressant therapies act on a common brain network. This network would be (i) derived from longitudinal pharmacotherapy, ECT, and MST experiments through therapeutic network mapping, (ii) validated by independent longitudinal datasets, (iii) annotated by depression-related genetic, molecular, and cognition networks, and (iv) tested for generalizability to DBS and rTMS.

---

## Results

Longitudinal experiments
A systematic search identified 298 studies investigating GMV changes after depression treatment (Supplementary Fig. 1; Supplementary Table 1). Ultimately, 15 studies with 16 independent experiments (11 ECT experiments, four pharmacotherapy experiments, and one MTS experiment) fulfilled our criteria. Here, a “study” refers to an individual scientific paper and an “experiment” indicates a single contrast of interest in a given study27. Data between experiments were independent. Collectively, these experiments included 533 depression patients (296 females; mean age ± standard deviation [SD], 54.66 ± 15.90 years) and 169 healthy controls (95 females; mean age ± SD, 43.70 ± 14.27 years) (Supplementary Table 2). Coordinates with longitudinal VBM changes in these experiments were used to map the therapeutic network of depression (see the study design in Fig. 1).

A common network modulated by distinct therapies
In the 16 experiments, we found 144 coordinates with increased GMV after treatment. These coordinates were heterogeneously distributed across the whole brain (Fig. 2a). We transformed these coordinates into experiment-specific networks using a local-to-network mapping method on a healthy functional connectome (Fig. 2b)25,26. All 16 networks showed common connectivity within a subregion of the left amygdala (100% overlap). More than 85% of experiments showed common connectivity with the bilateral insula, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and amygdala (termed the sensitivity map; Fig. 3a). Part of this common connectivity was specific to depression, compared to random networks and non-depression networks (termed the specificity maps; two-sample t-test family-wise error [FWE] corrected P < 0.05; Fig. 3b; Supplementary Tables 3–5; Supplementary Fig. 2). Conjunction analysis identified two clusters (termed hub regions) in the bilateral amygdala that were both sensitive (>85% in the sensitivity map) and specific to depression remission (P < 0.05 in both specificity maps, Fig. 3c). We computed the whole-brain connectivity network of these hub regions using the local-to-network mapping method (Fig. 3d). The resulting map indicated the common network in which regions were associated with depression remission, thus it was hereafter referred to as depression therapeutic network (DTN).

The whole-brain pattern of this DTN could be robustly identified when different sizes was used to define the seed spheres, when the connectome dataset changed, when GMV-decreased coordinates were also included as seeds, when studies with moderate or severe patients were analyzed separately, when ECT and non-ECT experiments were analyzed separately, when only psychiatry disorders were used in the specificity analysis, when different thresholds were used for sensitivity analysis, and when including five additional experiments in updating the experiment search in literature (see Supplementary Figs. 3–4).

Retrospective clinical validation
Group-level validation. GMV and cortical thickness (CTh) are two common measures of brain morphology. We did not use CTh studies to establish the DTN because the vertex-wise CTh analysis did not cover the subcortical structures and cerebellum. Here, the CTh findings were adopted as an independent validation dataset. In the literature, we identified CTh increases after treatment reported in five depression experiments and six non-depression experiments (Supplementary Figs. 5–6; Supplementary Tables 6–7). The networks of cortical regions where CTh increased after treatment were computed using local-to-network mapping for each experiment. The DTN showed higher spatial similarity with the networks in depression experiments (mean ± SD = 0.67 ± 0.17, two-sided one-sample t-test, t = 8.65, df = 4, P = 1 × 10−3, 95% CI = [0.4530, 0.8814]) than in non-depression experiments (mean ± SD = 0.11 ± 0.20, two-sided one-sample t-test, t = 1.35, df = 5, P = 0.236, 95% CI = [−0.0975, 0.3123]; two-sided two-sample t-test, t = 4.99, df = 9, P = 8 × 10−4, 95% CI = [0.3058, 0.8139]; Fig. 4a).

Individual-level validation. The individual-level validation analysis was implemented in two independent datasets (AHMU data, n = 40; USTC data, n = 54) of depression patients treated with ECT28 and a control group (21 Parkinson’s patients29). For each patient, we first identified the local areas showing increased GMV after treatment and then transformed the local changes into networks through local-to-network mapping. The networks in both depression cohorts exhibited significantly spatial correlation with the DTN (AHMU, mean ± SD = 0.39 ± 0.30, two-sided one-sample t-test, t = 8.16, df = 39, P = 1 × 10−4, 95% CI = [0.2921, 0.4846]; USTC, mean ± SD = 0.47 ± 0.30, two-sided one-sample t-test, t = 11.55, df = 53, P = 1 × 10-4, 95% CI = [0.3899, 0.5537]), while the control networks did not (mean ± SD = 0.14 ± 0.35, t = 1.89, df = 20, P = 0.07, 95% CI = [−0.0151, 0.3008]). The DTN showed a higher similarity to the depression networks than to the control networks (USTC cohort, two-sided two-sample t-test, t = 4.08, df = 73, P = 1 × 10−4, 95% CI = [0.1682, 0.4897]; AHMU cohort, two-sided two-sample t-test, t = 2.87, df = 59, P = 6 × 10−3, 95% CI = [0.0740, 0.4166]; Fig. 4b).

Prospective preclinical validation
To test the causal role of the DTN function in depression treatment, we designed a prospective treatment experiment with a rat model of depression. The model rats (n = 20) displayed typical depressive-like phenotypes as evidenced by the forced swimming test (FST; two-sided paired t-test, t = 12.87, df = 19, P = 8 × 10−11, 95% CI = [125.6, 174.5]; Fig. 5a). We randomly assigned the rats into an experimental group (n = 10) and a control group (n = 10). Amygdala function was temporally inhibited in the experimental group by injecting muscimol. The amygdala in the control group were injected with saline (Fig. 5b). After 5 days of electroconvulsive shock (ECS) treatment, we found a significant time-by-group interaction (F[1,16] = 29.88, P = 5 × 10−5, 95% CI = [79.3, 179.7]; Fig. 5b) for the immobility time in the FST. Post hoc analysis indicated that the treatment effect of ECS on immobility time (control group, post-ECS vs. pre-ECS t = 5.77, adjusted P = 6 × 10−5) was blocked by inhibiting amygdala function (experiment group, post-ECS vs. pre-ECS, t = 1.96, adjusted P = 0.13). We additionally performed three supplementary experiments on depressant rats. See the method and results in Supplementary Preclinical Experiment.

Genetic and molecular mechanism
To explore the genetic mechanism involved in depression treatment, we tested the spatial similarity between the DTN and networks of depression-risk genes. We adopted 218 depression-risk genes from the largest genome-wide meta-analysis study30. A transcriptomic map of these genes was computed using the “abagen” toolbox (v.0.1.3; https://github.com/rmarkello/abagen) and then transformed into networks through local-to-network mapping. Ninety of these networks showed significant spatial correlation with the DTN (P FDR < 0.05 after Moran’s test of spatial autocorrelation31; Fig. 6a, Supplementary Table 8). Enrichment analysis in Metascape (http://metascape.org) further indicated that these genes were significantly enriched in six ontology terms: “positive regulation of immune response”, “cell morphogenesis”, “regulation of response to biotic stimulus”, “spinal cord development”, “cell-cell adhesion”, and “platelet formation” (P FDR < 0.05). Additionally, the DTN showed significant spatial correlation with eight neurotransmitter networks (Fig. 6b): three dopamine transporter/receptor, two serotonin transporters/receptors, one noradrenaline transporter, one vesicular acetylcholine transporter, and one fluorodopa (P FDR < 0.05 after Moran’s test).

Cognition relevance
To explore the cognitive relevance of the DTN network, we investigated the spatial similarity between the DTN and 123 cognitive networks. We derived the activation maps of these cognitive terms using Neurosynth (https://github.com/neurosynth/neurosynth). Among the 123 cognitive networks, 21 and 24 networks showed significant positive correlation and anti-correlation with the DTN, respectively (P FDR < 0.05 after Moran’s test; Fig. 6c, Supplementary Table 9). Functions of the 21 positive networks were associated with psychomotor retardation (such as “movement”, “facial expression”, and “speech” terms). The 24 anti-correlated networks were associated with memory (such as “episodic memory”, “memory retrieval”, and “recognition” terms) and executive functions (such as “decision”, “intention”, and “strategy” terms)32.

Generalizability
The DTN was derived from pharmacotherapy, ECT, and MST experiments. We tested whether the DTN is also the target of other antidepressant therapies, such as DBS and TMS. In the literature, we found 11 effective brain sites for DBS33 and 13 for rTMS treatment33–35 (Supplementary Tables 10–11). These DBS sites showed stronger positive connectivity in the DTN (mean ± SD = 14.3 ± 7.7) than random networks (P = 0.008 in permutation tests; Fig. 7a). The rTMS targets showed stronger anti-correlation (mean ± SD = −11.1 ± 9.5) in the DTN than random networks (P < 0.005 in permutation tests; Fig. 7b). On longitudinal data of 24 major depression patients who received rTMS around the positive node of the DTN36, we found that functional connectivity changes within DTN were significantly correlated with symptom improvement as measured by the 17-item Hamilton Depression Scale (HAMD-17) (partial Pearson’s correlation r = 0.56, df = 16, P = 0.016; Fig. 7c). No significant correlation was found between the DTN change and improvement in other symptoms, including the Hamilton Anxiety Scale, Patient Health Questionnaire-15, Ruminative Response Scale, Pain Vigilance and Awareness Questionnaire, Insomnia Severity Index, and Temporal Experience of Pleasure Scale (Supplementary Table 12). These findings suggest that the DTN is specific to depression symptoms.

---

## Methods

This study was carried out under the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the institutional review board of Anhui Medical University and exempted from obtaining informed consent based on the secondary use of research data.

Literature search
We performed a systematic literature search for longitudinal studies investigating GMV changes in depression patients after clinical treatment. Coordinates with increased GMV after treatment were extracted for further analysis. The search followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines68 (see Supplementary Table 1 for the search strategy). The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) involving participants diagnosed with depression; (2) utilizing whole-brain VBM analyses; (3) reporting GMV longitudinal increases with treatment; (4) reporting coordinates in Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) or Talairach space; and (5) performing whole-brain correction for multiple comparisons. The exclusion criteria were (1) studies that did not report results in the form of standardized coordinates; (2) cross-sectional studies; (3) results that were not significant in longitudinal treatment; and (4) studies that were a review or a meta-analysis. Talairach coordinates were converted into MNI space using GingerALE software (version 3.0.2 www.brainmap.org).

We also checked the reference lists and review articles to identify studies that we may have missed. Two researchers independently searched these articles. In case of inconsistent opinions, the two researchers reached a consensus through discussion under the guidance of the corresponding author.

Therapeutic network mapping
The therapeutic network mapping method is an adaptation of lesion network mapping19. It comprises sensitivity, specificity, conjunction analyses, and network mapping. A critical method throughout these analyses is local-to-network mapping, which computes the brain network of local areas using a population-based functional connectome (Fig. 2b). The local areas refer to coordinates with GMV increases after depression treatment or to a whole-brain map weighted by other metrics, such as the density of a given neurotransmitter, or by the expression level of a given gene. The functional connectome comprised resting-state fMRI data of 652 healthy Chinese participants (termed the healthy connectome; mean age ± standard error = 22.9 ± 5.53 years old, 334 females)25. Acquisition and preprocessing of the fMRI data have been described previously29,69. Local-to-network mapping involved two steps. First, the average (or weighted average) signal of the local areas was correlated with that of each brain voxel using Pearson’s correlation on the functional connectome data. Then, a one-sample t-test was used to identify voxels that were significantly connected to the local areas (voxel-wise FWE-corrected P < 0.01). This t-map was defined as the brain network of the local areas.

Sensitivity analysis. We created spherical regions of interest (ROIs; 6 mm in diameter) centered at each coordinate reported by depression experiments, and combined multiple coordinates from one experiment to generate an experiment-specific seed image. All the experiment-specific seeds were transformed to networks by local-to-network mapping. These networks were binarized (voxel-wise FWE P < 0.01) and overlapped (i.e., summed and divided by the number of experiments) to show the common connections across all experiments. The sensitivity map refers to the resulting map with a 0.85 threshold.

Specificity analysis. To determine the connections specific to depression remission, we compared the networks from 16 depression experiments to two groups of control networks. One was from non-depression experiments. Coordinates with GMV increases after treatment (the inclusion criteria and search strategies are described in the Supplementary Methods) were transformed to networks through local-to-network mapping. The other group comprised random networks. These were networks of randomly redistributed seeds from the 16 depression experiments. The control networks were compared to 16 depression networks by 5000 permutation tests. A cluster-level P < 0.05 (with the cluster-forming threshold at voxel-level FWE P < 0.001) was considered statistically significant.

Conjunction analysis. Finally, we performed a conjunction analysis to identify regions that were both sensitive (connected to >85% of depression remission regions) and specific (voxels surviving specificity analyses) to depression remission, as in previous studies70,71. The regions identified by the conjunction analysis were hub regions for depression remission.

Network mapping. The resting-state functional connectivity of hub regions defines a human brain circuit that encompasses GMV changes causing depression remission. We derived this circuit using the hub regions as a seed through local-to-network mapping. We refer to this hub connectivity map as our DTN (a t-map with voxel-wise FWE P < 0.01).

Robustness analysis
Multiple control analyses were conducted to test the robustness of the DTN. First, to ensure that the DTN was independent of the seed size, we repeated the analysis using a larger sphere size of 10 mm. Second, to ensure that the DTN was independent of the connectome data used for the local-to-network mapping, we re-computed the DTN using an older healthy connectome (mean age ± SD = 55.45 ± 13.71; age range: 30–89) and a connectome of 365 patients with depression. We also re-computed the DTN separately for the depression patients in pre-treatment and post-remission stages (Supplementary Methods). Third, ECT accounted for more than half of the experiments (11 in 16) that we used for therapeutic network mapping. To ensure that the DTN was not solely driven by ECT coordinates, we re-computed the DTN using ECT and non-ECT experiments, respectively. Fourth, to ensure that the DTN was independent of the threshold of the sensitivity map, we re-computed the DTN using another two thresholds, 80 and 90%. Fifth, to examine whether the DTN exhibits distinct features across different stages of depression, we re-computed the DTN using data from studies on moderate and severe depression separately. The severity of depressive disorder in all available longitudinal experiments was assessed using the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD) or Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS). Depression severity was stratified according to the HAMD as moderate (scores, 17–23) and severe (scores, ≥24); according to the MADRS as moderate (scores, 20–34) and severe (scores, 35–60). Sixth, we re-performed the specificity analysis by restricting the control network to psychiatric disorders. Finally, we re-computed the DTN using seed images that combined both GMV-increased and -decreased coordinates. We also conducted an updated systematic literature search for longitudinal studies reporting GMV changes in patients with depression following clinical treatment, covering publications up to June 2025. More details of these robust analysis can be found in the Supplementary Tables 14–17.

Retrospective clinical validation
Group-level validation. We searched for longitudinal experiments investigating CTh changes after treatment (the inclusion criteria and detailed search strategies are described in the Supplemental Methods; Supplementary Tables 6–7) and classified them into depression and non-depression groups. Coordinates with increased CTh were extracted from these experiments and transformed into networks using local-to-network mapping. We hypothesized that the DTN would align more with the CTh networks in depression experiments than in non-depression experiments. To quantify this, we correlated the DTN with all CTh networks using spatial correlation (Pearson’s correlation) and compared the coefficient values between depression and non-depression groups using a two-sample t-test.

Individual-level validation. To validate the DTN at the individual level, we included longitudinal structural MRI data of depression (AHMU data, n = 40; USTC data, n = 54)28 and Parkinson’s disease (n = 21)29 from previous treatment studies. We first computed GMV changes after treatment using the SPM12 toolbox Computational Anatomy Toolbox12. We processed the data in the same way as in the previous study29. Then, the differential brain map of GMV (post-treatment vs. pre-treatment) of each patient was transformed into a network through local-to-network mapping. Finally, these networks were correlated with the DTN using voxel-wise spatial correlation (Pearson’s correlation). The correlation coefficients were compared between depression (AHMU and USTC data) and Parkinson’s disease groups using a two-sample t-test. We predicted that the DTN would have higher spatial similarity with the individual networks changed from depression treatment than from Parkinson’s disease treatment.

Prospective preclinical validation
Young male adult Sprague Dawley rats (6–8 weeks of age) were used for this experiment. First, the learned helplessness model was used to develop depression rats72, and the FST was used to assess the severity of depression. Over the next 5 days of treatment, we injected muscimol and saline to the bilateral basolateral amygdala for rats in the experimental and control groups, respectively. The injections were performed 30 min before each ECS. Finally, a post-treatment FST was performed 48 h after the last ECS. Ten rats each were allocated to the experimental and control groups. For detailed information regarding this main experiment and three supplementary experiments, see the Supplementary Preclinical Experiment.

Network annotation
Gene. We identified 269 risk genes of depression from the largest genome-wide association study (GWAS) for depression30. 218 of the 269 genes were available in the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA) (http://human.brain-map.org). In line with our previous studies67,73, gene expression maps were constructed from the left brain of AHBA using the “abagen” toolbox (v.0.1.3; https://github.com/abagen). The AHBA is based on 3702 spatially distinct samples from six post-mortem brains (age = 42.50 ± 13.38 years; male/female = 5/1) and includes expression maps of 218 depression-risk genes30. The microarray probes were re-annotated74, and probes that did not match a valid Entrez ID were discarded. Probes with intensity less than a background in ≥50.00% of samples across donors were discarded, yielding 31,569 probes. When multiple probes indexed the expression of the same gene, we selected the probe with the most consistent pattern of regional variation across donors (that is, with the highest differential stability)75. Gene expression values were then normalized across tissue samples using an identical procedure and computed in left-brain ROIs. These ROIs included 160 regions from the HCP-MMH atlas76 and nine cerebellum and four subcortical regions from the automatic anatomical labeling template77. We chose only ROIs in the left hemisphere because the microarray probes in the right hemisphere are not available in two of the AHBA brains. Samples assigned to the same ROI were averaged separately for each donor, and then across donors, yielding expression maps of 218 risk genes. These expression maps were transformed into brain networks through local-to-network mapping.

Neurotransmitter. Neurotransmitter density maps were obtained from previous positron emission tomography (PET) studies of healthy individuals, including dopamine receptors (D1R 78, D2R 55), serotonin receptors (5-HT1AR 79, 5-HT1BR 80, 5-HT2AR 80, 5-HT4R 80), a dopamine transporter (DAT 81), a serotonin transporter (SERT 80), fluorodopa (F-DOPA; a reflection of presynaptic dopamine synthesis capacity), a γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptor (GABAAR 81), a norepinephrine transporter (NAT 82), a vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT 55), and a metabotropic glutamate receptor type 5 (mGluR5 55). The distribution maps of neurotransmitter receptors/transporters were transformed into brain networks through local-to-network mapping.

Cognition. The neural correlates of different cognitive processes have been reported in many fMRI studies. A meta-analytic tool, Neurosynth, synthesized the findings in more than 15,000 studies searching for high-frequency keywords (https://github.com/neurosynth/neurosynth, using the volumetric association test maps83). In this study, we focused primarily on cognitive function and therefore limited the terms of interest to 123 cognitive or behavioral terms, which were selected from the Cognitive Atlas, a public ontology of cognitive science84. Terms ranged from umbrella terms (e.g., “memory”) to specific cognitive processes (e.g., “episodic memory”) and behaviors (e.g., “speech production”). The coordinates reported by Neurosynth in the Schaefer-100 atlas55,85 were transformed into brain networks through local-to-network mapping.

Null model for spatial correlation
The spatial correlation between networks was tested against a null model to correct for spatial autocorrelation using Moran’s test86 in the Neuromaps toolbox31 (https://github.com/netneurolab/neuromaps). Specifically, the spatial correlation was derived across 398 brain regions, including 360 cortical regions from the HCP-MMH atlas76 and 38 cerebellum and subcortical structures from an automatic anatomical labeling template77. A P-value was defined as the percentage of 5000 randomly permuted results that were stronger than the real result. Findings that survived Moran’s test were further corrected for FDR using the Benjamini–Hochberg method (PFDR) if multiple correlation analyses were performed.

Generalizability
We tested whether the 11 DBS and 13 rTMS sites aligned with the DTN by performing a permutation test. Specifically, we randomly redistributed the hub regions of DTN 2000 times and generated 2000 random networks through local-to-network mapping. We extracted the average value of the DBS and rTMS sites (spherical ROIs with a diameter of 6 mm) independently in these random networks. A P-value was defined as the percentage of 1000 random results that were stronger than the DTN.

To test whether the DTN can explain the outcome variability of depression treatment. We included 24 medical-refractory depression patients who received rTMS treatment from a previous study36. We computed the whole-brain functional connectivity (Pearson’s correlation) of the DTN (positive part) via rs-fMRI data before and following rTMS for each patient. The average functional connectivity changes within the DTN (positive part) were correlated with HAMD-17 improvement rates using partial Pearson’s correlation, controlling for age, gender, education, Hamilton Anxiety Scale, HAMA, and disease duration. To test the specificity, we also computed the correlations between the connectivity changes in the DTN and other symptom improvements using partial correlation analysis.

Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses were performed in MATLAB version 2018a (MathWorks). Image-based analyses were performed with SPM12 software (www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm), and the results were corrected for multiple comparisons in the whole brain. For all analyses, a two-sided P-value < 0.05 after correction was considered significant.

### Reviewer 1

The investigators of “Distinct antidepressant therapies act on a common brain network” assess structural brain changes associated with 16 unique ECT, MST, and pharmacotherapy investigations. These regions converged on a subregion of the left amygdala based on rs-fMRI from over 600 healthy controls labeled as the “depression remission network” (DRN). Retrospective validation included “spatial similarity” with cortical thickness changes and two independent ECT datasets. Prospective validation included a pre-translational mouse model with inhibited amygdala functioning, transcriptomic map of depression-risk genes, and cognitive relevance (activation maps from cognitive terms from Neurosynth). Finally, DBS and TMS targets aligned with DRN.
This well-written manuscript includes several strengths. The different layers (meta-analytic, genetic, cognitive, and pre-translational) and secondary analyses suggest convergence on the DRN. The remission network mapping also appears innovative.
Several considerations for review:
1. The manuscript is composed of secondary analyses. While this interesting from a hypothesis-generating perspective, this type of analyses does detract from the overall impact.
2. The selected nodes related are pre-/post-structural changes and not related to antidepressant outcomes. The ECT-imaging literature demonstrate that the ECT-mediated volumetric change is widely distributed but was not related to depression outcomes (see 2019 Ousdal Biological Psychiatry). The authors focus on volumetric change from ECT, MST, and pharmacotherapy, but these changes do not appear to be related to depression outcomes. Since this is the foundation for the development of the DRN, this may be a “shaky” foundation.
3. After selecting the nodes based on structural changes, the authors then use resting state fMRI from > 600 healthy controls to identify the anatomic area of convergence. Depressed patients may have different connectivity patterns both during and after the depressive episode that may not align with the DRN.
4. The pre-translational model simply demonstrates the widely accepted importance of the amygdala in depression and does not add any relevance to the “network”, which is based on the amygdala forming a hub of volumetric changes in discrete brain areas.
5. The genetic and cognitive relevance data do not provide direct support for the DRN.
6. The TMS experiments are interesting but were not used to prospectively test the role of a DRN “target”.

### Reviewer 2

This is a well-written manuscript that makes an interesting adaptation to the lesion network mapping method. The authors introduce "local-to-network mapping" by first identifying regions showing GMV increases following treatment in depression, then using these coordinates as seeds to identify hubs that change concurrently with the seed regions. The resulting hub—bilateral amygdala—was then used to identify a functional network related to treatment effect in the normative connectome, termed the "depressive remission network" (DRN). The authors validate the DRN for repeatability and disease specificity, and explore its correlation with gene expression and cognition. There are several methodological concerns require attention before its conclusions can be fully supported.
1.The authors' decision to focus exclusively on increased GMV as the local changes for DRN requires further justification. As noted in the introduction, different treatments produce bidirectional changes in brain volume. Why weren't both increased and decreased GMV sites included? While the authors mention conducting an analysis with GMV-decreased coordinates, these results are absent from both the main text and supplementary materials.
2.The study's treatment-related GMV increases derive predominantly from ECT studies, which typically involve treatment-resistant patients with severe depression, while pharmacotherapy studies generally include patients with milder symptoms. This fundamental clinical heterogeneity raises critical questions about the DRN's universality across the depression severity spectrum. Have the authors investigated whether the DRN hub architecture remains consistent between treatment responders and non-responders, or between severely and mildly depressed patients? This distinction is crucial for determining whether the identified network represents a universal depression remission pathway or merely reflects treatment-specific neuroplastic changes that vary with illness severity.
3.The age range of participants in studies reporting increased GMV was quite broad (30-70 years), while the normative connectome data came from individuals aged 20-30 years. Given the well-established impact of age on functional connectivity, how did the authors control for potential age-related confounds?
4.For the specificity validation, the authors compared the DRN with random networks and non-depression networks. It would be more informative to restrict the non-depression cohorts to other mood disorders, which would better clarify whether the depression remission network is specific to depression rather than mood disorders more broadly.
5.The authors link structural brain changes directly to therapeutic efficacy without empirically establishing this connection. When selecting studies showing GMV increases post-treatment, did they account for treatment response? Research like Redlich et al. (2016, JAMA Psychiatry) found that GMV increases didn't correlate with clinical improvement, suggesting these changes might be treatment byproducts rather than mechanisms. Why wasn't treatment response included in the review criteria? If non-responders show similar GMV changes as responders, these regions cannot legitimately constitute a 'remission network.' This raises the question: do treatment responders and non-responders share the same DRN architecture?"
6.For the MDD connectome data, please provide more detailed demographics, including disease duration, number of recurrent episodes, and medication status.
7.On page 16, line 408, under "prospective preclinical validation," supplementary preclinical experiments are mentioned but not included in the supplementary materials. Please provide this information.
8.Could the authors elaborate on the potential clinical significance and applications of this method? What insights does this study offer to the depression research community?

### Reviewer 3

This is a relevant study exploring the effect of common antidepressant therapies (pharmacotherapy, electroconvulsive therapy, and magnetic seizure therapy) in brain networks. The data presented provide new evidence about the neurobiological basis of antidepressant therapy.
I provide below a more detailed review of the preclinical experiment, as well as some additional general comments.
General:
1. It is not clear in the Abstract and Introduction section that this is actually a literature review study (i.e., secondary use of research data). This should be clearer mentioned for the reader in the beginning sections of the manuscripts.
2. Introduction, first paragraph: One additional aspect that could be highlighted is the delayed effect of antidepressant treatment, especially the pharmacotherapy.
3. Discussion, fifth paragraph: Study limitation is mentioned in terms of absence of studies evaluating psychotherapy and DBS adn rTMS that fulfilled the inclusion criteria, so that these aspects were not assessed in the present study. However, it looks like the literature search was performed on march/2022 and February-March/2023. I was wondering if some study fulfilling your criteria for these parameters was published after that.
Preclinical study:
The animal model for assessing depressive-like behaviors used the learned helplessness model (LHM) and forced swimming test (FST). Briefly, the LHM was used to develop depression in the rats, and the FST was used to assess the severity of depression. Some concerns are raised by this reviewer, especially regarding the experimental design.
1. Figure 5: Graph indicate 8-9 animals/group in Post-ECS data. However, n=10/group is mentioned in the text for this study. Accordingly, pre-ECS data have n=10/group. The authors should include detailed description in case some animals were lost along the protocol.
2. By the information provided in the text it looks like the animals in Pre-ECS condition were not subjected to BLA treatment (treatment onset was after that). If this is true, the data presentation should be reviewed since the way it is shown gives to the reader the wrong idea that the amygdala was inhibited both pre- and post-ECS.
3. A control group not subjected to ECS or BLA treatment is missing. This group would provide relevant information regarding the long-term depressive-like effect of LHM assessed in the FST. In other words, saline+ECS group presents a decrease in immobility, but how the authors can ensure that this decrease is not related to a progressive time-dependent reduction of the depressive-like effect caused by LHM. Please clarify.
4. The effect of repeated BLA treatment independent of ECS would also be relevant to provide information that the change in immobility in the FST is related to depressive-like behavior rather than an unspecific behavioral change in the FST.

### Reviewer 4

This manuscript identifies a network centered on the amygdala that the authors claim is specifically associated with symptomatic remission in depression across three therapeutic modalities: pharmacotherapy, magnetic seizure therapy, and electroconvulsive therapy. The study is impressively comprehensive. It builds upon data derived from a meta-analysis of multiple studies using longitudinal structural neuroimaging to assess brain changes associated with antidepressant treatments—potentially reflecting the neurobiological mechanisms of response. These data are then used for functional connectivity analyses employing robust, validated methods such as lesion network mapping. The authors further support their findings with a wide range of complementary analyses to test the robustness, generalizability, and specificity of the results, as well as preclinical studies aimed at deepening our understanding of the neurobiological mechanisms underlying treatment response. They also perform associations with gene expression maps, neurotransmitter distributions, and cognitive function profiles, thereby furthering a mechanistic interpretation of antidepressant efficacy.
Nonetheless, I have two major concerns that temper my enthusiasm for this work.
First, the brain regions identified by the authors as reactive to antidepressant treatment in the individual studies do not show—or at least are not shown to show—a significant association with clinical remission. This is particularly common in studies of electroconvulsive therapy (the most represented treatment modality in this analysis), where anatomical changes are often not reliably associated with clinical improvement. While I assume that clinical remission was significant in all studies included (this should be also explicitly reported), this does not necessarily imply that remission was related to the structural changes the authors selected as the basis for their analysis. In light of this, the term "remission network mapping" used by the authors becomes somewhat misleading.
Second, the authors appear to overlook a critical distinction between structural plasticity (changes in neuronal morphology) and functional plasticity (changes in synaptic efficacy). The study begins with structural changes and moves on to examine functional connectivity, implicitly treating both types of plasticity as two sides of the same coin. This equivalence is problematic. Structural plasticity is more readily observable in certain brain regions (for instance, limbic areas—where the authors find their effects—tend to exhibit detectable structural changes more easily than other cortical regions; see Butz et al., 2009; Kolb et al., 2003; Neufeld et al., 2009). This introduces a bias into the functional connectivity analyses and may obscure functional plasticity in other brain regions that could also be relevant for clinical response. These other regions could serve as seeds of interest from which to define functionally relevant networks more accurately associated with antidepressant effects.
Beyond these central concerns, I also have some reservations regarding the analytical strategies and their interpretation. For instance, I am not fully convinced that showing a higher similarity between maps derived from VBM and cortical thickness studies in depression—compared to other conditions—constitutes sufficient validation. While it is expected that such similarity might be greater in depression studies, this does not necessarily indicate meaningful convergence unless the magnitude and spatial distribution of the correlation are clearly reported and interpreted.
Likewise, I question the strategy of comparing networks derived from ECT vs. non-ECT studies to the overall network as a way of addressing potential confounding. Since this comparison involves a part-to-whole relationship, it likely inflates the correlation. Would it not be more appropriate to compare the ECT and non-ECT networks directly, rather than in relation to the network incorporating all treatment types?
Regarding the analysis of genetic and molecular mechanisms, the authors report a series of significant correlations, but these are only briefly discussed. The interpretation feels somewhat opportunistic—as though any significant result could have been included, regardless of its specific biological meaning.
Finally, the brain regions forming the core of the identified network are barely discussed. A more detailed description of these regions and their potential roles in depressive pathology would significantly enrich the discussion and provide valuable insight into the implications of the findings.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:

  2. Your original Round 1 review

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Depression disorder is a global health crisis, due to its high prevalence. Yet clinical treatments are inadequate. Uncovering the neural correlates of depression remission is a vital step toward developing effective therapies. Using a method termed therapeutic network mapping, we performed secondary analyses on the data of 16 longitudinal experiments and found that the network of the amygdala was commonly modulated by three antidepressant therapies (pharmacotherapy, electroconvulsive therapy, and magnetic seizure therapy). This therapeutic network was i) validated by two independent treatment datasets of patients with depression and a prospective preclinical experiment on male rats, ii) associated with networks of depression-related genes, neurotransmitters, and cognitions, and iii) also the target network of deep brain stimulation and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS). Finally, a longitudinal rTMS experiment indicated that strengthened therapeutic network connectivity is associated with higher depressant alleviation. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that distinct antidepressant therapies act on a common network with potential targets for developing effective therapies.

---

## Introduction

Depression disorder represents a severe global health crisis, owing to its high prevalence1,2. It is a leading contributor to disability and premature mortality in the world3,4. Pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy are first-line treatments for depression disorder. However, the therapeutic effects typically require weeks to months of continuous treatment to manifest, and approximately 30% of patients do not respond to these treatments5. These refractory patients need more intensive interventions6, such as electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), and magnetic seizure therapy (MST). Although these clinical therapies are effective, their mechanisms remain largely unknown.

Longitudinal imaging studies can provide important clues to understanding the remission mechanism of depression7. Relative to the highly variable workflows for functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)8, methods in structural studies are more homogeneous. However, the findings of such studies are inconsistent. For instance, MST was found to increase gray matter volume (GMV) in the bilateral paracentral lobule9, but ECT studies found restricted volume changes in the hippocampus–amygdala complex10,11 or widespread alterations in the brain12. The diversity of these findings between and within therapies has been a major obstacle to understanding the mechanism of depression remission. Regarding these findings as functionally isolated regions, coordinate-based meta-analytic approaches such as activation likelihood estimation are powerful tools for identifying the most consistent results13,14. Nonetheless, it is increasingly evident that brain regions linked to symptom remission are not acting in isolation. Rather, they are linked through distributed functional and structural brain circuits7,15–17. For instance, the targets of deep brain stimulation (DBS) and rTMS for depression belong to the same functional brain network18. Here, we hypothesized that the heterogeneous brain changes across different depression therapies aggregate in a common brain network.

Lesion network mapping is an effective way to determine the network effect of local changes19. This technique uses brain lesions as seeds to delineate the resting-state functional network of specific symptoms based on a normative connectome. This powerful and broadly applicable technique20 has been extended by replacing brain lesions with coordinates of brain structural atrophy21–23 and brain stimulation sites18,24 as seeds. Adapted from this technique, we propose a new method—called therapeutic network mapping—to identify the common network modulated by different therapies for depression. Briefly, we transformed the brain regions that longitudinally changed after treatment to networks through normative resting-state functional connectomes25,26 and explored the common connectivity across distinct therapies.

This study aimed to test whether distinct antidepressant therapies act on a common brain network. This network would be (i) derived from longitudinal pharmacotherapy, ECT, and MST experiments through therapeutic network mapping, (ii) validated by independent longitudinal datasets, (iii) annotated by depression-related genetic, molecular, and cognition networks, and (iv) tested for generalizability to DBS and rTMS.

---

## Results

Longitudinal experiments
A systematic search identified 298 studies investigating GMV changes after depression treatment (Supplementary Fig. 1; Supplementary Table 1). Ultimately, 15 studies with 16 independent experiments (11 ECT experiments, four pharmacotherapy experiments, and one MTS experiment) fulfilled our criteria. Here, a “study” refers to an individual scientific paper and an “experiment” indicates a single contrast of interest in a given study27. Data between experiments were independent. Collectively, these experiments included 533 depression patients (296 females; mean age ± standard deviation [SD], 54.66 ± 15.90 years) and 169 healthy controls (95 females; mean age ± SD, 43.70 ± 14.27 years) (Supplementary Table 2). Coordinates with longitudinal VBM changes in these experiments were used to map the therapeutic network of depression (see the study design in Fig. 1).

A common network modulated by distinct therapies
In the 16 experiments, we found 144 coordinates with increased GMV after treatment. These coordinates were heterogeneously distributed across the whole brain (Fig. 2a). We transformed these coordinates into experiment-specific networks using a local-to-network mapping method on a healthy functional connectome (Fig. 2b)25,26. All 16 networks showed common connectivity within a subregion of the left amygdala (100% overlap). More than 85% of experiments showed common connectivity with the bilateral insula, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and amygdala (termed the sensitivity map; Fig. 3a). Part of this common connectivity was specific to depression, compared to random networks and non-depression networks (termed the specificity maps; two-sample t-test family-wise error [FWE] corrected P < 0.05; Fig. 3b; Supplementary Tables 3–5; Supplementary Fig. 2). Conjunction analysis identified two clusters (termed hub regions) in the bilateral amygdala that were both sensitive (>85% in the sensitivity map) and specific to depression remission (P < 0.05 in both specificity maps, Fig. 3c). We computed the whole-brain connectivity network of these hub regions using the local-to-network mapping method (Fig. 3d). The resulting map indicated the common network in which regions were associated with depression remission, thus it was hereafter referred to as depression therapeutic network (DTN).

The whole-brain pattern of this DTN could be robustly identified when different sizes was used to define the seed spheres, when the connectome dataset changed, when GMV-decreased coordinates were also included as seeds, when studies with moderate or severe patients were analyzed separately, when ECT and non-ECT experiments were analyzed separately, when only psychiatry disorders were used in the specificity analysis, when different thresholds were used for sensitivity analysis, and when including five additional experiments in updating the experiment search in literature (see Supplementary Figs. 3–4).

Retrospective clinical validation
Group-level validation. GMV and cortical thickness (CTh) are two common measures of brain morphology. We did not use CTh studies to establish the DTN because the vertex-wise CTh analysis did not cover the subcortical structures and cerebellum. Here, the CTh findings were adopted as an independent validation dataset. In the literature, we identified CTh increases after treatment reported in five depression experiments and six non-depression experiments (Supplementary Figs. 5–6; Supplementary Tables 6–7). The networks of cortical regions where CTh increased after treatment were computed using local-to-network mapping for each experiment. The DTN showed higher spatial similarity with the networks in depression experiments (mean ± SD = 0.67 ± 0.17, two-sided one-sample t-test, t = 8.65, df = 4, P = 1 × 10−3, 95% CI = [0.4530, 0.8814]) than in non-depression experiments (mean ± SD = 0.11 ± 0.20, two-sided one-sample t-test, t = 1.35, df = 5, P = 0.236, 95% CI = [−0.0975, 0.3123]; two-sided two-sample t-test, t = 4.99, df = 9, P = 8 × 10−4, 95% CI = [0.3058, 0.8139]; Fig. 4a).

Individual-level validation. The individual-level validation analysis was implemented in two independent datasets (AHMU data, n = 40; USTC data, n = 54) of depression patients treated with ECT28 and a control group (21 Parkinson’s patients29). For each patient, we first identified the local areas showing increased GMV after treatment and then transformed the local changes into networks through local-to-network mapping. The networks in both depression cohorts exhibited significantly spatial correlation with the DTN (AHMU, mean ± SD = 0.39 ± 0.30, two-sided one-sample t-test, t = 8.16, df = 39, P = 1 × 10−4, 95% CI = [0.2921, 0.4846]; USTC, mean ± SD = 0.47 ± 0.30, two-sided one-sample t-test, t = 11.55, df = 53, P = 1 × 10-4, 95% CI = [0.3899, 0.5537]), while the control networks did not (mean ± SD = 0.14 ± 0.35, t = 1.89, df = 20, P = 0.07, 95% CI = [−0.0151, 0.3008]). The DTN showed a higher similarity to the depression networks than to the control networks (USTC cohort, two-sided two-sample t-test, t = 4.08, df = 73, P = 1 × 10−4, 95% CI = [0.1682, 0.4897]; AHMU cohort, two-sided two-sample t-test, t = 2.87, df = 59, P = 6 × 10−3, 95% CI = [0.0740, 0.4166]; Fig. 4b).

Prospective preclinical validation
To test the causal role of the DTN function in depression treatment, we designed a prospective treatment experiment with a rat model of depression. The model rats (n = 20) displayed typical depressive-like phenotypes as evidenced by the forced swimming test (FST; two-sided paired t-test, t = 12.87, df = 19, P = 8 × 10−11, 95% CI = [125.6, 174.5]; Fig. 5a). We randomly assigned the rats into an experimental group (n = 10) and a control group (n = 10). Amygdala function was temporally inhibited in the experimental group by injecting muscimol. The amygdala in the control group were injected with saline (Fig. 5b). After 5 days of electroconvulsive shock (ECS) treatment, we found a significant time-by-group interaction (F[1,16] = 29.88, P = 5 × 10−5, 95% CI = [79.3, 179.7]; Fig. 5b) for the immobility time in the FST. Post hoc analysis indicated that the treatment effect of ECS on immobility time (control group, post-ECS vs. pre-ECS t = 5.77, adjusted P = 6 × 10−5) was blocked by inhibiting amygdala function (experiment group, post-ECS vs. pre-ECS, t = 1.96, adjusted P = 0.13). We additionally performed three supplementary experiments on depressant rats. See the method and results in Supplementary Preclinical Experiment.

Genetic and molecular mechanism
To explore the genetic mechanism involved in depression treatment, we tested the spatial similarity between the DTN and networks of depression-risk genes. We adopted 218 depression-risk genes from the largest genome-wide meta-analysis study30. A transcriptomic map of these genes was computed using the “abagen” toolbox (v.0.1.3; https://github.com/rmarkello/abagen) and then transformed into networks through local-to-network mapping. Ninety of these networks showed significant spatial correlation with the DTN (P FDR < 0.05 after Moran’s test of spatial autocorrelation31; Fig. 6a, Supplementary Table 8). Enrichment analysis in Metascape (http://metascape.org) further indicated that these genes were significantly enriched in six ontology terms: “positive regulation of immune response”, “cell morphogenesis”, “regulation of response to biotic stimulus”, “spinal cord development”, “cell-cell adhesion”, and “platelet formation” (P FDR < 0.05). Additionally, the DTN showed significant spatial correlation with eight neurotransmitter networks (Fig. 6b): three dopamine transporter/receptor, two serotonin transporters/receptors, one noradrenaline transporter, one vesicular acetylcholine transporter, and one fluorodopa (P FDR < 0.05 after Moran’s test).

Cognition relevance
To explore the cognitive relevance of the DTN network, we investigated the spatial similarity between the DTN and 123 cognitive networks. We derived the activation maps of these cognitive terms using Neurosynth (https://github.com/neurosynth/neurosynth). Among the 123 cognitive networks, 21 and 24 networks showed significant positive correlation and anti-correlation with the DTN, respectively (P FDR < 0.05 after Moran’s test; Fig. 6c, Supplementary Table 9). Functions of the 21 positive networks were associated with psychomotor retardation (such as “movement”, “facial expression”, and “speech” terms). The 24 anti-correlated networks were associated with memory (such as “episodic memory”, “memory retrieval”, and “recognition” terms) and executive functions (such as “decision”, “intention”, and “strategy” terms)32.

Generalizability
The DTN was derived from pharmacotherapy, ECT, and MST experiments. We tested whether the DTN is also the target of other antidepressant therapies, such as DBS and TMS. In the literature, we found 11 effective brain sites for DBS33 and 13 for rTMS treatment33–35 (Supplementary Tables 10–11). These DBS sites showed stronger positive connectivity in the DTN (mean ± SD = 14.3 ± 7.7) than random networks (P = 0.008 in permutation tests; Fig. 7a). The rTMS targets showed stronger anti-correlation (mean ± SD = −11.1 ± 9.5) in the DTN than random networks (P < 0.005 in permutation tests; Fig. 7b). On longitudinal data of 24 major depression patients who received rTMS around the positive node of the DTN36, we found that functional connectivity changes within DTN were significantly correlated with symptom improvement as measured by the 17-item Hamilton Depression Scale (HAMD-17) (partial Pearson’s correlation r = 0.56, df = 16, P = 0.016; Fig. 7c). No significant correlation was found between the DTN change and improvement in other symptoms, including the Hamilton Anxiety Scale, Patient Health Questionnaire-15, Ruminative Response Scale, Pain Vigilance and Awareness Questionnaire, Insomnia Severity Index, and Temporal Experience of Pleasure Scale (Supplementary Table 12). These findings suggest that the DTN is specific to depression symptoms.

## Methods

This study was carried out under the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the institutional review board of Anhui Medical University and exempted from obtaining informed consent based on the secondary use of research data.

Literature search
We performed a systematic literature search for longitudinal studies investigating GMV changes in depression patients after clinical treatment. Coordinates with increased GMV after treatment were extracted for further analysis. The search followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines68 (see Supplementary Table 1 for the search strategy). The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) involving participants diagnosed with depression; (2) utilizing whole-brain VBM analyses; (3) reporting GMV longitudinal increases with treatment; (4) reporting coordinates in Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) or Talairach space; and (5) performing whole-brain correction for multiple comparisons. The exclusion criteria were (1) studies that did not report results in the form of standardized coordinates; (2) cross-sectional studies; (3) results that were not significant in longitudinal treatment; and (4) studies that were a review or a meta-analysis. Talairach coordinates were converted into MNI space using GingerALE software (version 3.0.2 www.brainmap.org).

We also checked the reference lists and review articles to identify studies that we may have missed. Two researchers independently searched these articles. In case of inconsistent opinions, the two researchers reached a consensus through discussion under the guidance of the corresponding author.

Therapeutic network mapping
The therapeutic network mapping method is an adaptation of lesion network mapping19. It comprises sensitivity, specificity, conjunction analyses, and network mapping. A critical method throughout these analyses is local-to-network mapping, which computes the brain network of local areas using a population-based functional connectome (Fig. 2b). The local areas refer to coordinates with GMV increases after depression treatment or to a whole-brain map weighted by other metrics, such as the density of a given neurotransmitter, or by the expression level of a given gene. The functional connectome comprised resting-state fMRI data of 652 healthy Chinese participants (termed the healthy connectome; mean age ± standard error = 22.9 ± 5.53 years old, 334 females)25. Acquisition and preprocessing of the fMRI data have been described previously29,69. Local-to-network mapping involved two steps. First, the average (or weighted average) signal of the local areas was correlated with that of each brain voxel using Pearson’s correlation on the functional connectome data. Then, a one-sample t-test was used to identify voxels that were significantly connected to the local areas (voxel-wise FWE-corrected P < 0.01). This t-map was defined as the brain network of the local areas.

Sensitivity analysis. We created spherical regions of interest (ROIs; 6 mm in diameter) centered at each coordinate reported by depression experiments, and combined multiple coordinates from one experiment to generate an experiment-specific seed image. All the experiment-specific seeds were transformed to networks by local-to-network mapping. These networks were binarized (voxel-wise FWE P < 0.01) and overlapped (i.e., summed and divided by the number of experiments) to show the common connections across all experiments. The sensitivity map refers to the resulting map with a 0.85 threshold.

Specificity analysis. To determine the connections specific to depression remission, we compared the networks from 16 depression experiments to two groups of control networks. One was from non-depression experiments. Coordinates with GMV increases after treatment (the inclusion criteria and search strategies are described in the Supplementary Methods) were transformed to networks through local-to-network mapping. The other group comprised random networks. These were networks of randomly redistributed seeds from the 16 depression experiments. The control networks were compared to 16 depression networks by 5000 permutation tests. A cluster-level P < 0.05 (with the cluster-forming threshold at voxel-level FWE P < 0.001) was considered statistically significant.

Conjunction analysis. Finally, we performed a conjunction analysis to identify regions that were both sensitive (connected to >85% of depression remission regions) and specific (voxels surviving specificity analyses) to depression remission, as in previous studies70,71. The regions identified by the conjunction analysis were hub regions for depression remission.

Network mapping. The resting-state functional connectivity of hub regions defines a human brain circuit that encompasses GMV changes causing depression remission. We derived this circuit using the hub regions as a seed through local-to-network mapping. We refer to this hub connectivity map as our DTN (a t-map with voxel-wise FWE P < 0.01).

Robustness analysis
Multiple control analyses were conducted to test the robustness of the DTN. First, to ensure that the DTN was independent of the seed size, we repeated the analysis using a larger sphere size of 10 mm. Second, to ensure that the DTN was independent of the connectome data used for the local-to-network mapping, we re-computed the DTN using an older healthy connectome (mean age ± SD = 55.45 ± 13.71; age range: 30–89) and a connectome of 365 patients with depression. We also re-computed the DTN separately for the depression patients in pre-treatment and post-remission stages (Supplementary Methods). Third, ECT accounted for more than half of the experiments (11 in 16) that we used for therapeutic network mapping. To ensure that the DTN was not solely driven by ECT coordinates, we re-computed the DTN using ECT and non-ECT experiments, respectively. Fourth, to ensure that the DTN was independent of the threshold of the sensitivity map, we re-computed the DTN using another two thresholds, 80 and 90%. Fifth, to examine whether the DTN exhibits distinct features across different stages of depression, we re-computed the DTN using data from studies on moderate and severe depression separately. The severity of depressive disorder in all available longitudinal experiments was assessed using the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD) or Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS). Depression severity was stratified according to the HAMD as moderate (scores, 17–23) and severe (scores, ≥24); according to the MADRS as moderate (scores, 20–34) and severe (scores, 35–60). Sixth, we re-performed the specificity analysis by restricting the control network to psychiatric disorders. Finally, we re-computed the DTN using seed images that combined both GMV-increased and -decreased coordinates. We also conducted an updated systematic literature search for longitudinal studies reporting GMV changes in patients with depression following clinical treatment, covering publications up to June 2025. More details of these robust analysis can be found in the Supplementary Tables 14–17.

Retrospective clinical validation
Group-level validation. We searched for longitudinal experiments investigating CTh changes after treatment (the inclusion criteria and detailed search strategies are described in the Supplemental Methods; Supplementary Tables 6–7) and classified them into depression and non-depression groups. Coordinates with increased CTh were extracted from these experiments and transformed into networks using local-to-network mapping. We hypothesized that the DTN would align more with the CTh networks in depression experiments than in non-depression experiments. To quantify this, we correlated the DTN with all CTh networks using spatial correlation (Pearson’s correlation) and compared the coefficient values between depression and non-depression groups using a two-sample t-test.

Individual-level validation. To validate the DTN at the individual level, we included longitudinal structural MRI data of depression (AHMU data, n = 40; USTC data, n = 54)28 and Parkinson’s disease (n = 21)29 from previous treatment studies. We first computed GMV changes after treatment using the SPM12 toolbox Computational Anatomy Toolbox12. We processed the data in the same way as in the previous study29. Then, the differential brain map of GMV (post-treatment vs. pre-treatment) of each patient was transformed into a network through local-to-network mapping. Finally, these networks were correlated with the DTN using voxel-wise spatial correlation (Pearson’s correlation). The correlation coefficients were compared between depression (AHMU and USTC data) and Parkinson’s disease groups using a two-sample t-test. We predicted that the DTN would have higher spatial similarity with the individual networks changed from depression treatment than from Parkinson’s disease treatment.

Prospective preclinical validation
Young male adult Sprague Dawley rats (6–8 weeks of age) were used for this experiment. First, the learned helplessness model was used to develop depression rats72, and the FST was used to assess the severity of depression. Over the next 5 days of treatment, we injected muscimol and saline to the bilateral basolateral amygdala for rats in the experimental and control groups, respectively. The injections were performed 30 min before each ECS. Finally, a post-treatment FST was performed 48 h after the last ECS. Ten rats each were allocated to the experimental and control groups. For detailed information regarding this main experiment and three supplementary experiments, see the Supplementary Preclinical Experiment.

Network annotation
Gene. We identified 269 risk genes of depression from the largest genome-wide association study (GWAS) for depression30. 218 of the 269 genes were available in the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA) (http://human.brain-map.org). In line with our previous studies67,73, gene expression maps were constructed from the left brain of AHBA using the “abagen” toolbox (v.0.1.3; https://github.com/abagen). The AHBA is based on 3702 spatially distinct samples from six post-mortem brains (age = 42.50 ± 13.38 years; male/female = 5/1) and includes expression maps of 218 depression-risk genes30. The microarray probes were re-annotated74, and probes that did not match a valid Entrez ID were discarded. Probes with intensity less than a background in ≥50.00% of samples across donors were discarded, yielding 31,569 probes. When multiple probes indexed the expression of the same gene, we selected the probe with the most consistent pattern of regional variation across donors (that is, with the highest differential stability)75. Gene expression values were then normalized across tissue samples using an identical procedure and computed in left-brain ROIs. These ROIs included 160 regions from the HCP-MMH atlas76 and nine cerebellum and four subcortical regions from the automatic anatomical labeling template77. We chose only ROIs in the left hemisphere because the microarray probes in the right hemisphere are not available in two of the AHBA brains. Samples assigned to the same ROI were averaged separately for each donor, and then across donors, yielding expression maps of 218 risk genes. These expression maps were transformed into brain networks through local-to-network mapping.

Neurotransmitter. Neurotransmitter density maps were obtained from previous positron emission tomography (PET) studies of healthy individuals, including dopamine receptors (D1R 78, D2R 55), serotonin receptors (5-HT1AR 79, 5-HT1BR 80, 5-HT2AR 80, 5-HT4R 80), a dopamine transporter (DAT 81), a serotonin transporter (SERT 80), fluorodopa (F-DOPA; a reflection of presynaptic dopamine synthesis capacity), a γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptor (GABAAR 81), a norepinephrine transporter (NAT 82), a vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT 55), and a metabotropic glutamate receptor type 5 (mGluR5 55). The distribution maps of neurotransmitter receptors/transporters were transformed into brain networks through local-to-network mapping.

Cognition. The neural correlates of different cognitive processes have been reported in many fMRI studies. A meta-analytic tool, Neurosynth, synthesized the findings in more than 15,000 studies searching for high-frequency keywords (https://github.com/neurosynth/neurosynth, using the volumetric association test maps83). In this study, we focused primarily on cognitive function and therefore limited the terms of interest to 123 cognitive or behavioral terms, which were selected from the Cognitive Atlas, a public ontology of cognitive science84. Terms ranged from umbrella terms (e.g., “memory”) to specific cognitive processes (e.g., “episodic memory”) and behaviors (e.g., “speech production”). The coordinates reported by Neurosynth in the Schaefer-100 atlas55,85 were transformed into brain networks through local-to-network mapping.

Null model for spatial correlation
The spatial correlation between networks was tested against a null model to correct for spatial autocorrelation using Moran’s test86 in the Neuromaps toolbox31 (https://github.com/netneurolab/neuromaps). Specifically, the spatial correlation was derived across 398 brain regions, including 360 cortical regions from the HCP-MMH atlas76 and 38 cerebellum and subcortical structures from an automatic anatomical labeling template77. A P-value was defined as the percentage of 5000 randomly permuted results that were stronger than the real result. Findings that survived Moran’s test were further corrected for FDR using the Benjamini–Hochberg method (PFDR) if multiple correlation analyses were performed.

Generalizability
We tested whether the 11 DBS and 13 rTMS sites aligned with the DTN by performing a permutation test. Specifically, we randomly redistributed the hub regions of DTN 2000 times and generated 2000 random networks through local-to-network mapping. We extracted the average value of the DBS and rTMS sites (spherical ROIs with a diameter of 6 mm) independently in these random networks. A P-value was defined as the percentage of 1000 random results that were stronger than the DTN.

To test whether the DTN can explain the outcome variability of depression treatment. We included 24 medical-refractory depression patients who received rTMS treatment from a previous study36. We computed the whole-brain functional connectivity (Pearson’s correlation) of the DTN (positive part) via rs-fMRI data before and following rTMS for each patient. The average functional connectivity changes within the DTN (positive part) were correlated with HAMD-17 improvement rates using partial Pearson’s correlation, controlling for age, gender, education, Hamilton Anxiety Scale, HAMA, and disease duration. To test the specificity, we also computed the correlations between the connectivity changes in the DTN and other symptom improvements using partial correlation analysis.

Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses were performed in MATLAB version 2018a (MathWorks). Image-based analyses were performed with SPM12 software (www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm), and the results were corrected for multiple comparisons in the whole brain. For all analyses, a two-sided P-value < 0.05 after correction was considered significant.

While I assume that clinical remission was significant in all studies included (this should be also explicitly reported), this does not necessarily imply that remission was related to the structural changes the authors selected as the basis for their analysis. In light of this, the term "remission network mapping" used by the authors becomes somewhat misleading.
Second, the authors appear to overlook a critical distinction between structural plasticity (changes in neuronal morphology) and functional plasticity (changes in synaptic efficacy). The study begins with structural changes and moves on to examine functional connectivity, implicitly treating both types of plasticity as two sides of the same coin. This equivalence is problematic. Structural plasticity is more readily observable in certain brain regions (for instance, limbic areas—where the authors find their effects—tend to exhibit detectable structural changes more easily than other cortical regions; see Butz et al., 2009; Kolb et al., 2003; Neufeld et al., 2009). This introduces a bias into the functional connectivity analyses and may obscure functional plasticity in other brain regions that could also be relevant for clinical response. These other regions could serve as seeds of interest from which to define functionally relevant networks more accurately associated with antidepressant effects.
Beyond these central concerns, I also have some reservations regarding the analytical strategies and their interpretation. For instance, I am not fully convinced that showing a higher similarity between maps derived from VBM and cortical thickness studies in depression—compared to other conditions—constitutes sufficient validation. While it is expected that such similarity might be greater in depression studies, this does not necessarily indicate meaningful convergence unless the magnitude and spatial distribution of the correlation are clearly reported and interpreted.
Likewise, I question the strategy of comparing networks derived from ECT vs. non-ECT studies to the overall network as a way of addressing potential confounding. Since this comparison involves a part-to-whole relationship, it likely inflates the correlation. Would it not be more appropriate to compare the ECT and non-ECT networks directly, rather than in relation to the network incorporating all treatment types?
Regarding the analysis of genetic and molecular mechanisms, the authors report a series of significant correlations, but these are only briefly discussed. The interpretation feels somewhat opportunistic—as though any significant result could have been included, regardless of its specific biological meaning.
Finally, the brain regions forming the core of the identified network are barely discussed. A more detailed description of these regions and their potential roles in depressive pathology would significantly enrich the discussion and provide valuable insight into the implications of the findings.
